Good taste is about really seeing the big patterns and kind of instinctively knowing what's the right way to do things.

People who understand pointers just use a "pointer to the entry pointer", and initialize that with the address of the list_head. And then as they traverse the list, they can remove the entry without using any conditionals, by just doing a "*pp = entry->next".

I say "no good reason", because there *is* a reason for it: it allows code to avoid the special case of empty list and adding entries to before the first entry etc etc.  But that reason is a really *bad* reason, because it's valid only because people don't understand basic list manipulation and pointers to pointers.

Special case code is bad. It's certainly a lot more important to me to have a straightforward approach that doesn't have any strange cases, and where debugging "just works", instead of having a lot of magic small details scattered all over the place.
Random special cases in code are just evil, and end up biting us in the end.

The proper fix in that case (in my opinion, and the one that thus got committed ;^) was simply to make sure that the data structures were simply always consistent (and empty), even if the code itself was disabled. That just automatically meant that it didn't need any global flags to be tested.

For suspend, the only other case we've seen has been the keyboard and mouse controller, which has exactly the same "we can special case it with a single 'let's do _this_ device asynchronously'". Again, it may not be pretty, but it sure is simple.
And then we'd limit the special case to where it matters (with a big comment about what's going on), rather than adding random special case handling to random _other_ places.
In fact, I'm a huge proponent of designing your code around the data, rather than the other way around, and I think it's one of the reasons git has been fairly successful (*).

(*) I will, in fact, claim that the difference between a bad programmer and a good one is whether he considers his code or his data structures more important. Bad programmers worry about the code. Good programmers worry about data structures and their relationships.

I think the code got less understandable, and had more special cases, just because now we have two totally different kinds of deltas. So maybe I'm reacting to the fact that I think the bug happened in the first place for a very simple reason: the data structure wasn't unambiguous any more.
the way to do good basic design isn't actually to be really smart about it, but to try to have a few basic concepts.
I think that if we have a value that we need, then it should be recorded. In the data structures. Not in some random other location that isn't part of the real git data structures.
a willingness to not abstract away the data structures and algorithms, because those are the *whole*point* of core git.
It's really that the crypto interfaces are *designed* so that you have to allocate things separately, and can't embed these things in your own data structures.
You should not hide algorithmic choices in your data structures. You should make them explicit, so that when you read the code you _see_ what assumptions people make.
Marking data structures is seriously stupid and wrong. It's not the *data* that has access rules, it's the *code* that has rules of access.
I hate hiding locks in "helper functions". You search for the lock, and now you've hidden that "siglock" usage away and made it very different from all the other siglock usage.
abstraction like this is _bad_, for christ sake! Don't hide what locks you're using just to make the code look simpler.
But I'm also a huge believer in *explicit*syntax*. People should see what is going on, and the abstraction should be explicit.
The advantage of READ_ONCE() over using "volatile" in a data structure tends to be that you explicitly mark the memory accesses that you care about.
I do NOT understand why you seem to argue for being "subtle" and "clever", considering the history of this whole setup. Subtle and clever and complex is what got us to the crap situation.

Any time people do ad-hoc locking with "clever" schemes, it's almost invariably buggy. So the rule is: just don't do that. Make the locking rules "obvious".  Don't have subtle rules about "if head is NULL, then we're not going to add any new buffers to it, except if tail is also NULL".
So at some point I just decided that "optimal" was less important than "simple to think about".

Overdesigning is a disease. It's fundamentally wrong.

Adding these kinds of "abstraction layers" is something that people are taught is good, but I personally tend to think that it makes it less obvious at the code level what the "costs" are. Unless you know things intimately, you really have no way of judging whether "fpath_inode()" is something expensive or not.
Over-abstraction is a real problem - it makes the code less obvious, and if there is no real gain from it then over-abstracting things is a bad thing.
Good abstraction has zero performance penalty, and can make the system much more pleasant to work with. And I claim that this is the DEFINITION of good abstraction.
If this was something where we'd expect things to change in the future, maybe it would be worth it for _that_ reason.

Dammit, if we add wrapper and "helper" functions, they should *help*, not confuse.

I'm not arguing against those kinds of wrappers that actually _clarify_ things. I'm arguing against random wrappers that don't, and that really fundamentally seem like they cannot possibly ever have any other valid value.
And there are downsides to arbitrary random wrappers/helpers. Churn. Harder to see what the code actually *does*.

Helper functions with one single use-case shouldn't be helper fucntions. They should be inlines in the one single file that uses them. Trying to make up abstraction layers is not "helping", it's just making code harder to read, and trying to convince people to use specialized helpers just causes more cognitive load.
Helper wrappers that are just used once or twice can still be nice readability improvements just because they make each part be easier to read on its own.
But again - keep that helper if you want it. Just don't put a badly implemented and badly named "helper" it in a global header file that _everybody_ has to look at.
Basically, dense lines are bad. And ?: can make for code that ends up "too dense".
Basically, lines-of-code is a completely bogus metric for _anything_. Including maintainability.
make an inline function that has a descriptive name. It's still complex, but now the complexity is _described_, and not mixed in with potentially other complex actions.
It might not _always_ be a win size and performance-wise, but it can be, and so readability should generally always be the #1 goal, because quite often it actually does help the compiler too.
See if the code flow makes sense from 10,000 feet - you can pick up overlong functions and various other dubious practices really clearly (#ifdef's in code etc).

name things for the _concept_, not for some odd implementation issue

I dislike #ifdef code.  Avoid it whenever possible.  #ifdefs become ugly, and destroy the linearity of the code (== hard to read).

I hate code that has #ifdef's. It's a major design mistake, and shows that the person who coded it didn't think of it as _one_ problem, but as two.

Having the #ifdef's outside the code tends to have two advantages: - it makes the code much more readable, and doesn't split things up. - you have to choose your abstraction interfaces more carefully, which in turn tends to make for better code.

#ifdef's in code is not about syntax, it's about abstraction. This is still the exact same thing as having an #ifdef around it, and in many ways it is *worse*, because now it's just made to look somewhat different with a particularly ugly #ifdef.
